guideline.title: Point-of-care testing in general haematology: An update to the British Society for Haematology good practice paper
guideline.citation: Tam J, De la Salle B, Kapuya P, Reilly-Stitt C, Smith-Straney T, Cambridge T, et al. Br J Haematol. 2026;209(4):1489–1504.
guideline.overview: This update to the 2019 BSH POCT guideline covers point-of-care testing in secondary care. Community POCT will be addressed separately. It has two halves: the analytical strengths and limits of each device class (FBC/Hb, PT/INR, ACT, D-dimer, viscoelastic, DOAC, blood gas Hb, platelet function, fibrinogen, haemoglobinopathy and G6PD), and the service framework. That framework covers QA (IQC and EQA), ISO 15189:2022 accreditation (which now absorbs ISO 22870), governance, training, finance, device selection, health and safety, reflex testing, incident reporting (including SHOT), data protection and record retention. Device-specific thresholds are needed wherever devices vary from one another.

recommendations.text: Device-specific thresholds should be established for ACT tests, given the variability between tests.
Only high-sensitivity D-dimer tests with performance matching STA® or ELISA laboratory assays should be used.
Validation of viscoelastic assays should involve establishment of clinical decision-making algorithms and reference ranges.
Blood gas analysers should not substitute laboratory-based testing of Hb/Hct but may aid in monitoring trends or making immediate clinical judgements.
Where interfacing of results from POCT to a laboratory information management system (LIMS) exists, this should be utilised in real time to prevent transcription errors.

The POCT QA framework should include: oversight and monitoring by a laboratory professional or quality manager; internal quality control (IQC) and external quality assessment (EQA) processes; an internal audit schedule; accreditation to ISO 15189 by the appointed national accreditation bodies; document control including standard operating procedures (SOPs); regular review of the service by senior management for continual improvement.
The POCT policy must describe governance, quality assurance and risk management arrangements for the implementation of a new test or device.

Where devices or tests may not meet traditional quality and governance requirements (e.g. emerging technologies or methodologies, absence of a laboratory comparator), formal risk assessment must be undertaken. Identified risk must be mitigated where reasonably practicable.
A structured training programme (theoretical and practical) for all POCT personnel and end users must be developed and maintained by the POCT manager or training and development coordinator.
All training materials (structured syllabi) must be alongside a competency assessment, to be completed and passed before first use. A training manual may ensure a structured approach.
Before training or assessing end users, POCT personnel must first demonstrate a higher level of understanding of the test process, application and performance.
A separate training and competency document must be maintained and updated whenever a point-of-care test or device changes.
Training complexity and competency is proportional to the clinical application of the test or process.
Training and competency assessment should cover expertise required to safely provide results for patient care.
Users must demonstrate competence in device operation, methodological theory, pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical factors, and result validity.
A financial framework should detail the cost-effectiveness and financial value in POCT provision as an alternative or complementary to the medical laboratory.
Recruitment should cover the necessary business skills to manage and develop the service as a business unit, or these skills should be developed internally.
Clinical and medical effectiveness: Devices must demonstrate clear clinical utility by supporting diagnosis, treatment and patient management, ideally within established care pathways.

Economic evaluation: Economic impacts of devices should be assessed before adoption, including cost-effectiveness (per diagnosis or outcome), LOS reduction and workforce improvements, including productivity and satisfaction.
Patient safety and blood conservation: Devices should minimise blood volume requirements.
Safety and ergonomics: Devices must incorporate biohazard containment, safe disposal (sharps and waste), user-friendly design and risk reduction mechanisms.

Technical quality and reliability: Devices should have proven technical robustness and be amenable to automated calibration, reliable throughput, reagent stability, minimal pre- and post-analytical steps (where possible), accreditation and user training.

Analytical performance verification: Each device must be verified for accuracy, level of imprecision compared to the 'gold standard' method, reproducibility, linearity and stability across the measurement range. Results must be comparable with CL standards and include error detection, interference warnings and specimen flagging capabilities.

Data management and systems integration: Devices must support secure, long-term, interoperable data management and storage, for example, bidirectional connectivity, remote access, automated critical result alerts, EHR integration.
Device qualification: An ISO 15189:2022-compliant acceptance process must include verification protocols, method comparisons and training and competency requirements.
Staff must have up-to-date training and competency assessments and participate in risk assessments and audits.
Needle-stick injuries must be reported, for example, via Datix reporting system.
There must be disposal procedures for sharps, blood-stained material, reagents and electronic waste.
A no-blame reporting culture to encourage incident reporting without fear of reprisal, supporting transparency and safety improvement.
Regular training on incident reporting (focusing on 'how' and 'when'), for all POCT users, to support clarity and confidence in the reporting system.
Clear reporting responsibilities embedded in SOPs specifying who should report, what should be reported and how to escalate concerns.
Proactive reporting to inform service improvements and targeted retraining, to prevent recurrence.
Routine audits of incident data to identify trends, share organisation-wide learnings and strengthen governance.
Incidents that impact on transfusion practice should be reported to the Serious Hazards of Transfusion (SHOT) haemovigilance scheme.
Secure, traceable, auditable digital documentation using centralised POCT management software, to reduce the risk of data loss or unauthorised access.
A document control system to ensure that only current, approved versions of policies, logs and reports are in use, precluding outdated versions.
Training for all POCT users to cover data protection, confidentiality, GDPR requirements and NHS DSP Toolkit standards.
Data access logs, audited at defined intervals to monitor inappropriate access or breaches and demonstrate data governance compliance.
Secure destruction of expired paper records (e.g. cross-cut shredding, approved confidential waste disposal) in line with the NHS Records Management Code of Practice.
Compliance with GDPR, NHS DSP Toolkit and local information security policies should be overseen by an information governance lead or POCT data controller.
Patient test results should be retained for at least 8 years after the last patient contact, in line with NHS record-keeping requirements.
Calibration records, QC logs and equipment maintenance reports are kept for a locally documented period (usually at least 5 years) to support audits, accreditation and incident investigations.
Training and competency records should be retained for at least 5 years to evidence staff authorisation and compliance.
Device-specific analytical and clinical thresholds should be established where interdevice variability is demonstrated.
POCT services must operate a QA programme that includes IQC and participation in EQA.
SOPs must be made available to and followed by all POCT staff.
POCT patient results must be retained permanently (electronic or paper records) and clearly identified as a POCT result in the patient record.
A structured programme of training, competency assessment and re-certification must be implemented for all POCT users.
A financial framework must be developed to demonstrate cost-effectiveness and financial value of POCT services.
Adverse incidents must always be reported, including near misses and events not resulting in patient harm.
Centralised POCT management software should be implemented to ensure secure, traceable, auditable digital documentation.
POCT records must be stored securely and retained for defined, policy-compliant retention periods.

topics.name: What POCT is, scope and ISO 15189:2022
topics.why: The definition, the scope (secondary care only) and the standards change (ISO 22870 absorbed into ISO 15189:2022) are basic exam facts.
keyPoints: **POCT** is diagnostic testing **outside the hospital laboratory, close to the patient**, with results available quickly enough to **influence immediate clinical management**.

Recent drivers: innovation, **stronger frameworks**, and **digital integration and connectivity** (devices linked to LIMS and EHRs, allowing data transfer and remote monitoring). **COVID-19 accelerated decentralised testing.**

**ISO 15189:2022** sets requirements for quality, governance and risk in medical laboratories, and **now includes POCT requirements** previously covered by **ISO 22870:2016**, which is **superseded** (a few organisations may still hold ISO 22870 accreditation).
**Scope:** a framework for high-quality POCT in **secondary care**. **Community POCT is out of scope** and will be addressed separately.
POCT can speed patient flow and inform immediate treatment in life-threatening situations. It may sit within a wider operational efficiency strategy, **with the approval of a POCT committee**.

Literature: PubMed searches in **January 2025**, covering Aug 2019 to Jan 2025, plus 2009–2025 for fibrinogen, ROTEM/TEG and EQA. **683 articles** were identified. Sickle cell, malaria, HIV, HbA1c, hCG and TB were **excluded** from the searches.
pitfalls: ISO 22870 is no longer the POCT standard. POCT is now accredited under ISO 15189:2022 as part of the laboratory (by UKAS in the UK).

selfTest.q: Which standard now covers POCT requirements, and which did it replace?
selfTest.a: ISO 15189:2022, which incorporates and supersedes ISO 22870:2016.

selfTest.q: Is community POCT covered by this paper?
selfTest.a: No. It covers secondary care, and community POCT will be addressed separately.

topics.name: Device classes: FBC, Hb, haemoglobinopathy and G6PD (Table 1)
topics.why: Table 1 sets out the principle, use and main limitation of each POCT technology, and these are often examined as matching items.
keyPoints: **Portable Hb analysers** (i-STAT, **HemoCue Hb 201+**, EKF DiaSpect) use **spectrophotometry**. Results come in **1–3 minutes** and are highly reproducible, but they are **affected by lipaemia and icterus**. **HemoCue cannot measure Hct directly** (it estimates it from Hb). Uses: virtual wards, theatres, clinics, GP surgeries, blood donation.

**Impedance FBC** (Coulter principle, e.g. Sysmex pocH-100i, PixCell HemoScreen) uses simple, established hardware but gives only a **limited differential** (3- or 5-part). Uses: virtual wards, ED, theatres, GP surgeries, community and **clozapine clinics**.

**Five-part impedance with microfluidics plus AI imaging** (e.g. PixCell HemoScreen, Sysmex XN-L) gives high resolution with minimal user input and can be **interfaced bidirectionally** (technical validation in the central laboratory and real-time reporting). Drawbacks are **higher cost per test** and dependence on **cartridge supply**. These can detect cell abnormalities and are **recommended for haematology clinics**.
FBC POCT analysers have been shown to give **accurate, reproducible results** against central laboratory instruments in venous and capillary samples.
**HemoTypeSC** is a **lateral flow** immunoassay with antibodies to **HbA, HbS and HbC**. It detects **HbSS and HbSC**, but **not other significant variants**.

**Gazelle (Hemex)** is **microchip cellulose acetate electrophoresis**, used to screen for **β-thalassaemia trait**. Sensitivity and specificity are high, but **confirmatory testing is required**, and **cellulose acetate is not reliable for quantitation**. Cation-exchange HPLC identifies variants by retention time.

**G6PD POCT** (e.g. STANDARD G6PD) is **quantitative and enzymatic**, measuring NADPH production at **340 nm normalised to Hb**. It is **confounded by sex and reticulocyte count**, and results vary between laboratories, so **harmonisation** is needed.

**D-dimer and fibrinogen** POCT use **turbidimetric or latex agglutination** immunoassays (light scattering from antigen–antibody complexes), e.g. Radiometer AQT90, i-STAT, LumiraDx, Exdia TRF, Cobas h232, Triage.

**ClotPro** is a viscoelastic device in which the **cup rotates and the pin is still**. With the **ECA** test it detects **dabigatran and argatroban**, and with the **RVV** test it detects **enoxaparin, rivaroxaban and apixaban**. It is limited in decentralised settings and **cannot always separate anticoagulant classes**.

pitfalls: HemoTypeSC will miss HbD, HbE, β-thalassaemia and other variants. It only detects A, S and C.
A normal G6PD POCT result during reticulocytosis (e.g. after haemolysis) may be falsely reassuring, because reticulocytes have higher G6PD activity.
topics.hook: Hb is light, FBC is resistance, HemoTypeSC is a strip, Gazelle is a gel, G6PD is 340 nm.

selfTest.q: Which interferences affect portable spectrophotometric Hb analysers?
selfTest.a: Lipaemia and icterus (high lipids or bilirubin).

selfTest.q: What does the Gazelle device screen for, and what is its limitation?
selfTest.a: β-thalassaemia trait, by microchip cellulose acetate electrophoresis. Confirmatory testing is required, and cellulose acetate is not reliable for quantitation.

selfTest.q: Which factors confound POCT G6PD activity?
selfTest.a: Sex (gender) and reticulocyte count. Inter-laboratory variability also means harmonisation is needed.

topics.name: Coagulation POCT: INR, ACT, D-dimer and DOACs
topics.why: Each coagulation POCT has a specific failure mode, such as APS on warfarin, ACT confounders, low-sensitivity D-dimers and DOACs that can be ruled out but not measured.
keyPoints: **PT/INR POCT** (CoaguChek Pro II/XS, Xprecia Prime, i-STAT, microINR, LumiraDx, and smartphone-based devices) uses **thromboplastin activation with electrochemical or electromechanical detection**. It is quick and needs a small volume.

INR limits: **clinically significant discrepancies in APS patients on warfarin**; **monitor bias between test strips at INR ≥4**; within a **stable INR of 2–4**, POCT is comparable to laboratory INR up to 4. **Unsuitable with lupus anticoagulant or very high INR.**

**ACT** (i-STAT ACTk, Hemochron) monitors **UFH in cardiac surgery and ECMO**. It correlates with anti-Xa in non-cardiac arterial procedures and with incomplete protamine reversal. But **hypothermia, haemodilution and platelet count and function** dissociate ACT from heparin effect. On bypass it correlates poorly with anti-Xa if there is **lupus anticoagulant (prolonged APTT)** or **raised heparin–VWF**. i-STAT is more reproducible than Hemochron, so **device-specific thresholds** are needed.
**D-dimer** is used with a **clinical probability score** (Wells, Geneva, PERC) and **age-adjusted** ranges to rule out DVT and PE. Laboratory assays are latex or ELISA (VIDAS).

POCT D-dimers (Cobas, Triage, AFIAS-1, Standard F200, LumiraDx, HP-AFS/1, Exdia TRF Plus): **Triage is comparable to VIDAS**, and several had **false-negative rates <1.4%** against STA-Liatest. But a meta-analysis found **slightly lower sensitivity** than laboratory assays, so use them **only in low-risk populations**. **Qualitative assays have limited utility** because of low sensitivity and quality issues.

**DOAC POCT:** routine monitoring is unnecessary, but levels help in **stroke, bleeding, urgent surgery and before thrombolysis**. **DTM, DOASENSE, CoaguChek and TEG 6S cannot quantify DOACs**, but may **rule out clinically relevant levels (<30–50 ng/mL)**.

**DTM test card:** 95–97% sensitivity for dabigatran >30 and >50 ng/mL. **DOASENSE urine dipstick:** sensitivity **100% for dabigatran** and **97% for anti-Xa agents** at ≥30 ng/mL. **CoaguChek INR:** >95% specificity for edoxaban >30 and >50 ng/mL. **TEG 6S DOAC algorithm:** 98–100% sensitivity for Xa and IIa inhibitors, 100% specificity.
numbers: INR at which strip-to-strip bias must be monitored
stable INR window where POCT is comparable to the laboratory
false-negative rate of several POCT D-dimer platforms
DOAC levels POCT can help rule out
DOASENSE sensitivity: dabigatran / anti-Xa at ≥30 ng/mL
pitfalls: Do not use POCT INR in antiphospholipid syndrome or with lupus anticoagulant. Use the laboratory INR.
A qualitative POCT D-dimer is not suitable for excluding VTE. Use only high-sensitivity assays that match STA or ELISA performance (1B).
A cold, haemodiluted bypass patient may have a prolonged ACT that reflects hypothermia and dilution, not heparin.
topics.hook: INR fails in APS and at INR ≥4. ACT is fooled by Cold, Dilution and Platelets. A D-dimer must be High-sensitivity. A DOAC can be ruled out but not measured.

selfTest.q: In which patients is POCT INR unreliable?
selfTest.a: APS or lupus anticoagulant, and very high INRs (monitor strip bias at INR ≥4).

selfTest.q: Which factors dissociate ACT from the anticoagulant effect of UFH?
selfTest.a: Hypothermia, haemodilution, and platelet count and function. On bypass, also lupus anticoagulant or raised heparin–VWF.

selfTest.q: What can POCT DOAC tests do, and what can they not do?
selfTest.a: They cannot quantify DOACs, but they can rule out clinically relevant levels (<30–50 ng/mL).

topics.name: Viscoelastic, platelet function and fibrinogen POCT
topics.why: These devices guide transfusion in bleeding. Know which predict bleeding (Multiplate) and which do not (PFA screening).
keyPoints: **Viscoelastic assays** are vital in bleeding from **trauma, cardiac surgery and obstetrics**, and are also used in liver disease, ED and **ECMO**. Devices: **TEG, ROTEM, Quantra (ultrasound), Sonoclot, ClotChip, ClotPro**. Designs: cup and pin, ultrasonic, cartridge.

Quantra, TEG 6S and ROTEM Sigma **correlate strongly** with laboratory platelet and fibrinogen tests. Quantra and ROTEM perform similarly in trauma-induced coagulopathy, **ROTEM is better for hypofibrinogenaemia**, and **Quantra is faster**. Viscoelastic algorithms give **modest outcome improvements** in bleeding.

**NICE** recommends **TEG and ROTEM in cardiac surgery**, and **Sonoclot only in research**. **ISO 15189:2022 (section 7.3.5)** requires **device-specific algorithms and reference ranges** for viscoelastic tests.
**Platelet function POCT:** PFA-100/200, **VerifyNow**, **Multiplate**, PL-11, PlateletWorks, Smart Clot, and TEG platelet mapping.
**PFA screening is non-specific**: it **cannot distinguish VWD from platelet function defects**, and **non-selective screening does not predict bleeding or transfusion** before invasive procedures.

**Multiplate predicts perioperative bleeding and transfusion in cardiac surgery** and **outperformed TEG in CABG** (bleeding, transfusion, re-exploration). A meta-analysis (**39 studies, n=4101**) supports it but notes **inter-device variability**, which makes common decision limits difficult. The PL-11 comparison showed marked inter-device variability.

**Fibrinogen POCT:** **qLabs FIB** (electrical impedance), **FibCare and F-Point** (light scattering) are **comparable to Clauss**. They are useful in transfusion, haemorrhage and gynaecological surgery.
**TEG CFF and ROTEM FIBTEM** detect hypofibrinogenaemia and may guide treatment in **postpartum and surgical bleeding**.
numbers: meta-analysis supporting Multiplate in cardiac surgery
ISO 15189:2022 section requiring viscoelastic algorithms and ranges
pitfalls: A prolonged PFA closure time cannot tell VWD from a platelet defect, and routine pre-operative PFA screening does not predict bleeding.
Viscoelastic thresholds are device-specific. Do not apply ROTEM cut-offs to TEG.
topics.hook: Multiplate Predicts, PFA Fails to predict. FIBTEM and CFF find low fibrinogen.

selfTest.q: Which POCT platelet test best predicts bleeding after cardiac surgery?
selfTest.a: Multiplate (multiple electrode impedance aggregometry). It outperformed TEG in CABG.

selfTest.q: What does NICE say about viscoelastic devices?
selfTest.a: TEG and ROTEM are recommended in cardiac surgery. Sonoclot is recommended only in research.

selfTest.q: What must viscoelastic validation include?
selfTest.a: Clinical decision-making algorithms and reference ranges (1B; ISO 15189:2022 §7.3.5).

topics.name: Blood gas Hb/Hct and LIMS interfacing
topics.why: Blood gas Hb is used all the time to decide on transfusion, but it is not interchangeable with laboratory Hb.
keyPoints: Blood gas analysers measure **Hb spectrophotometrically** and **Hct by conductivity or calculation**.
They analyse **whole blood**, so **haemolysis usually cannot be detected**. Consider it when results are unexpected or discordant.

Some studies show agreement with laboratory Hb, but **underestimation** of Hb/Hct can trigger **unnecessary transfusion**. In one study, **21%** of patients who would have been transfused on laboratory Hct would **not** have been on blood gas Hct. **Systematic overestimation** (mean **8 g/L**) has also been reported.
By **CLIA interchangeability criteria**, blood gas analysers are **not interchangeable** with laboratory analysers for Hb.
Use blood gas Hb for **trends and immediate decisions**, **not as a substitute** for laboratory Hb/Hct.
Where POCT results can be **interfaced to the LIMS**, use the interface **in real time** to **prevent transcription errors**.
numbers: patients whose transfusion decision differed between laboratory and blood gas Hct
mean overestimation of Hb by blood gas in one study
pitfalls: Blood gas Hb can be wrong in either direction. Confirm in the laboratory before a non-urgent transfusion.
Poor mixing or partial clotting of blood gas samples causes inaccurate Hb. SHOT has reported inappropriate transfusions and TACO from this.
topics.hook: Gas for trends, laboratory for transfusion.

selfTest.q: Can blood gas Hb replace laboratory Hb?
selfTest.a: No (1C). Blood gas analysers are not interchangeable with laboratory analysers under CLIA criteria. Use them for trends and immediate judgements.

selfTest.q: Why can haemolysis be missed on a blood gas Hb?
selfTest.a: Blood gas analysers test whole blood, so there is no plasma to inspect for haemolysis.

topics.name: Quality assurance: IQC, EQA, audit and SOPs
topics.why: The QA framework is the core of a safe POCT service. Know the six elements and how IQC differs from EQA.
keyPoints: QA covers **pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical** stages, and includes training, personnel, equipment and **appropriateness of testing**.

POCT should be **integrated into the central laboratory quality management system**, with the same standards of leadership, training, competency, IT, procurement and governance. A **quality manual** is not essential for accreditation but is helpful.

**IQC** controls **accuracy, within- and between-day variability, drift and bias**, using controls near **clinical decision thresholds**. Base frequency on testing activity, analyse drift at locally defined intervals, and make lot numbers, targets and results **fully traceable**.

Use **third-party QC** where possible. Run IQC **after maintenance or calibration** and for **new reagent lots (batch acceptance)**. Have an **IQC failure policy** and a **contingency plan** for system failure.

**EQA** provides samples of **known but undisclosed** concentration, at decision levels and across linearity. It **complements but does not replace IQC**. It gives peer comparison (by device or method), a long-term retrospective view, and supports **post-market surveillance**.
Document EQA results and the response to **out-of-consensus** results. A statistically out-of-consensus result **may not be clinically significant**: interpret it in context.

If no EQA exists: **interlaboratory exchange of blinded samples** within a trust, or **simultaneous venous and capillary sampling** across devices, with limits of agreement that reflect **physiological differences**. Periodic comparison with central laboratory methods is good practice.

**POCT users are not laboratory scientists.** Encourage regular users (not just experienced or laboratory staff) to run IQC and EQA. EQA material often differs from clinical samples, which causes errors. Training mitigates this.

**Audit:** an internal audit schedule covering all aspects, with corrective and preventive actions fed into policy. In the UK, hospital POCT is **accredited by UKAS as part of the clinical laboratory**.
**SOPs** must meet **ISO 15189** structure and content (Figure 1). File results **permanently**, **clearly identified as POCT**.
pitfalls: EQA does not replace IQC. You need both.
Out-of-consensus does not always mean clinically wrong. Assess clinical significance and long-term performance.
topics.hook: IQC = every day, inside, catches drift. EQA = periodic, outside, compares you with peers.

selfTest.q: List the six elements of the POCT QA framework (1B).
selfTest.a: Oversight by a laboratory professional or quality manager; IQC and EQA; an internal audit schedule; ISO 15189 accreditation; document control including SOPs; senior management review for continual improvement.

selfTest.q: What alternatives exist when no EQA scheme is available for a device?
selfTest.a: Interlaboratory exchange of blinded samples within the trust, and simultaneous venous and capillary sampling across devices, with locally set limits of agreement.

topics.name: Governance and training
topics.why: No POCT device should be adopted without governance, and training and competency carry many of the strongest (1A) recommendations.
keyPoints: **POCT devices must not be adopted without a well-defined governance structure** and clear accountability for every element of the service.
Most POCT is part of an **accredited pathology laboratory** under clinical directorship. Day-to-day running may be delegated to a **POCT coordinator or manager**.

A multidisciplinary **POCT committee** is helpful but **not mandatory under ISO 15189:2022**. Members: clinicians, laboratory scientists, nurses, support staff, management, the POCT coordinator, **IT, Estates and Clinical Engineering**, with finance and procurement advice. It is accountable to a higher governance group. If POCT extends to the community, include **community representation** (pharmacist, GP or practice nurse).
If no committee is feasible, effectiveness must still be shown through the **POCT policy** and its evidence. Services outside an accredited organisation need a **Service Level Agreement**.
**Training (Figure 2):** **mandatory retraining intervals** must be stated in a policy that is **signed off at a high level** and is enforceable on all users.
Training must be **auditable**, with audits **at least annually** and more often for higher-risk tests or poor-performance trends. Improvement draws on feedback, audit, trends and incident reports.

Competency must be **passed before first use**. Trainers must show a **higher level of understanding** first. Update documentation **whenever a test or device changes**. Training complexity should be **proportional** to the clinical application.
numbers: minimum audit frequency for training and competency
pitfalls: A POCT committee is not mandatory under ISO 15189:2022, but governance, accountability and a POCT policy are.
New technologies without a laboratory comparator still need a formal risk assessment (1B).
topics.hook: No governance, no gadget. Train, test, then use.

selfTest.q: Is a POCT committee mandatory under ISO 15189:2022?
selfTest.a: No. But governance must be demonstrated through the POCT policy, with clear accountability.

selfTest.q: What must users demonstrate competence in (1A)?
selfTest.a: Device operation, methodological theory, pre-analytical, analytical and post-analytical factors, and result validity.

topics.name: Finance and choosing devices
topics.why: Business cases and the device selection criteria (Menendez-Botet) are less familiar, but they are recommended at 1B.
keyPoints: POCT was once seen as more expensive, but analyses suggest an **overall financial benefit**. Count **costs avoided** as well: cancellations, unnecessary appointments, readmissions, **length of stay**, imaging and theatre time. A **major driver of savings is staff time**.

Know the **true cost** (Figure 3), and work with procurement and performance teams. Leads need **business acumen** and must produce **business cases** that quantify risk to patient care and the benefit of POCT.
**Managed service partnerships** with industry can reduce risk, but efficiencies must be weighed against **patient outcomes**.

Device selection: review the product literature and specifications, with **on-site demonstration and evaluation**. **Minimise blood loss** (neonates and anaemic patients), because frequent sampling causes **iatrogenic anaemia** and transfusion.

Selection and verification follow the **Menendez-Botet criteria**: clinical effectiveness; economic evaluation; blood conservation; safety and ergonomics; technical quality; analytical verification (accuracy, imprecision vs gold standard, reproducibility, linearity, stability, error detection, interference warnings, flagging); data management (bidirectional connectivity, remote access, critical result alerts, EHR); and **ISO 15189:2022-compliant acceptance**.
pitfalls: Comparing cost per test alone undervalues POCT. Include avoided costs such as length of stay and staff time.
topics.hook: Menendez-Botet's 8: Clinical, Economic, Blood-saving, Safe, Technical, Analytical, Data, Qualification.

selfTest.q: Whose criteria guide selection and verification of POCT devices?
selfTest.a: Menendez-Botet.

selfTest.q: What is a major driver of cost savings from POCT?
selfTest.a: Optimising staff time, along with avoided costs such as reduced length of stay and fewer cancellations.

topics.name: Health and safety, reflex testing and incident reporting
topics.why: POCT errors are a recognised cause of inappropriate transfusion, and SHOT reporting is a frequent exam point.
keyPoints: **Table 2, health and safety:** **biological** (PPE, sharps, treat all blood as infectious); **infection control** (hand hygiene, disinfect between patients, clean and dirty zones, single-use consumables); **chemical** (COSHH, storage, spill kits); **electrical** (**annual PAT testing**, keep devices dry and clean, servicing, remove damaged devices).
Documentation (SOPs, risk and COSHH assessments, QC logs, service records) must align with **MHRA**, **ISO 15189:2022** and **CQC** requirements.

**Reflex testing** is a protocol-driven follow-up test without a separate order. Example: **HemoCue Hb <80 g/L** leads to automatic **FBC and ferritin** in the central laboratory. Benefits: fewer delays, protocol adherence, better flow, fewer missed diagnoses (e.g. thrombocytopenia, sepsis). It needs governance, SOPs, and **training for escalation and override**.

**Adverse incidents (Table 3):** device malfunction (false Hb or INR); operator error (low volume, expired reagents, not following SOPs); **testing despite out-of-range QC**; connectivity failures; cross-contamination; **missed reflex testing or failure to escalate critical values**; **sample misidentification**; and **errors causing avoidable, delayed or inappropriate transfusion**.
Report promptly for trend analysis and for compliance with the **MHRA Yellow Card scheme**, ISO 15189:2022 and CQC.

**SHOT** reports include poor blood gas sample preparation (**inadequate mixing, partial clotting**) leading to wrong Hb, **inappropriate transfusion and TACO**. Transfusion-related POCT errors **must be reported to SHOT**.

Reporting is **everyone's responsibility** (clinicians, BMS, laboratory assistants, pharmacists). **Report even if there is no harm.** Ongoing risks go on the **Risk Register**, which may lead to business cases.

rows: False high or low Hb or INR
Insufficient volume, expired reagents, SOP not followed

Missed reflex test, critical value not escalated
Poor blood gas practice leading to an inappropriate transfusion decision

numbers: example HemoCue Hb that triggers reflex FBC and ferritin
pitfalls: Near misses and no-harm events must still be reported (1A).
Transfusion-related POCT errors go to SHOT, not just the local incident system.
topics.hook: No harm still means report. Transfusion harm means report to SHOT.

selfTest.q: Give an example of reflex testing from the paper.
selfTest.a: A HemoCue Hb below 80 g/L automatically triggers an FBC and ferritin in the central laboratory.

selfTest.q: Which blood gas sampling errors has SHOT highlighted, and what harm can follow?
selfTest.a: Inadequate mixing and partial clotting, giving inaccurate Hb. This can lead to inappropriate transfusion and TACO.

topics.name: Data protection and record retention
topics.why: The retention periods (8 years for results, 5 years for QC and training records) are specific, testable numbers.
keyPoints: POCT data must comply with **GDPR** and the **NHS Data Security and Protection (DSP) Toolkit**. Keep it confidential, protect its integrity, collect the **minimum necessary**, store it securely, archive it and destroy it eventually. Use encryption, passwords, firewalls and audit trails.

Maintain: **centralised POCT management software** (secure, traceable, auditable); **document control**; **data protection training** for all users (1A); **audited access logs**; **secure destruction** of paper (cross-cut shredding) per the **NHS Records Management Code of Practice**; and oversight by an **information governance lead or POCT data controller**.

**Retention:** patient results for **at least 8 years after the last patient contact**; calibration, QC and maintenance records for a local period, **usually at least 5 years**; **training and competency records at least 5 years**.

**Summary:** a high-quality service depends on technology, leadership, defined pathways, training and QA, **embedded in an accredited framework** to the **same standards as laboratory testing**. The **Infected Blood Inquiry's** safety culture informed the guideline.
numbers: after last patient contact: patient results
QC, calibration and maintenance records (usual local period)
pitfalls: The 8-year period runs from the last patient contact, not from the date of the test.

The paper is internally inconsistent here. The storage section says results are kept for at least 8 years (store-1), but the key recommendations say POCT results must be 'retained permanently' in the record and labelled as POCT (key-4). Know both, and quote whichever fits the question.

selfTest.q: How long should POCT patient results be retained?
selfTest.a: At least 8 years after the last patient contact (1B).

selfTest.q: How long should training and competency records be kept?
selfTest.a: At least 5 years (1B).
